{"id": "3:83/q08", "question": "How are the seeking and returning verbs read?", "turns_on": "Person and voice of each verb, and which reader uses each form.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q08/p1", "position": "Both are read in the second person, directly addressing the audience.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī prefers continuity with the prior address; al-Fārisī cites 3:84. Al-Rāzī says the address can include believers and unbelievers."}, {"id": "3:83/q08/p2", "position": "Both are read in the third person, reporting rejecters or transgressors.", "reasons": "Ḥafṣ is repeatedly named, with Yaʿqūb, Sahl, and others in varying assignments; 3:82 supports the reference. Al-Khalawayh says God expresses wonder to the Prophet; Ibn al-Jawzī unusually calls it the majority reading."}, {"id": "3:83/q08/p3", "position": "The first is third person, the return second person, moving from specific rejecters to everyone's return.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAmr is usually assigned this mixed form. Al-Khalawayh prefers its breadth; al-Ṭabarī permits the person shift. Sources specify vowels differently."}, {"id": "3:83/q08/p4", "position": "The first is second person, the return third person, shifting from addressed rejecters to all accountable beings.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī and al-Rāzī attribute this to Abū ʿAmr, contrary to many other assignments."}, {"id": "3:83/q08/p5", "position": "The return may be passive second person, 'you are returned,' or active third person, 'they return'.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER contrasts imposed return with subjects portrayed as returning; Asad gives literal passive force. Al-Bayḍāwī notes the yāʾ form may refer back to 'whoever'."}, {"id": "3:83/q08/p6", "position": "Some notes register yāʾ and tāʾ variation without complete or consistent reader assignments.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid's excerpt names no readers; al-Nashr lists third-person readers at a related locus."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q09", "question": "What does aslama mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether it denotes obedience, recognition, irresistible created dependence, or another Qur'anic sense of Islam.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q09/p1", "position": "It means submitted, obeyed, yielded, or humbled oneself.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba likens entering submission to entering a season and cites 4:94; Ibn al-Jawzī equates istislām. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, and others gloss compliance and abasement; other Qur'anic examples include 10:90, 27:44, and 37:103."}, {"id": "3:83/q09/p2", "position": "It means recognition of God's lordship, creatorhood, and human servanthood, even without sincere worship.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Sinān gloss knowledge; Mujāhid invokes 29:61, 31:25, 39:38, and 43:87. Al-Ḍāmghānī compares outward profession in 49:14 and 9:74. Abū al-ʿĀliya contrasts sincerity with associating partners."}, {"id": "3:83/q09/p3", "position": "It means subjection to God's creative governance and decree, which no creature can evade.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Kaysān invoke created constitution; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses the past tense and willing/unwilling contrast, distinguishing creational from devotional Islam. Al-Ṭabarī also speaks of humbling and exclusive lordship."}, {"id": "3:83/q09/p4", "position": "Islam can elsewhere mean professed religion, monotheism, sincerity, or outward acknowledgment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī cites 3:19, 22:78, 5:44, 2:131, 3:20, 31:22, 9:74, and 49:14. The Ḥadīth of Gabriel and Ibn Abī Shayba distinguish outward Islam from inward faith; al-Burhān relates al-Salām and al-Muʾmin; al-Ḍāmghānī also lists greeting among salām's senses."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q10", "question": "How may the adjacent mīms in 'aslama man' be pronounced?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q10/p1", "position": "The first mīm may optionally assimilate into the following mīm.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās notes the optional assimilation."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q11", "question": "Who are those in the heavens and the earth?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is exhaustive or particularly refers to named groups.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q11/p1", "position": "The phrase includes all created inhabitants: angels in heaven and humans and jinn on earth.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says man includes angels, humans, and jinn; al-Nasafī and Study Quran identify the inhabitants. Al-Biqāʿī includes those with bodily and intellectual defensive power."}, {"id": "3:83/q11/p2", "position": "Heavenly submitters are angels; earthly willing groups include the Emigrants, Helpers, ʿAbd al-Qays, Banū Sulaym, or Bahrainis.", "reasons": "The lists differ: the Prophetic report names Helpers and ʿAbd al-Qays; al-Ḥasan and Maṭar add or omit Emigrants, Banū Sulaym, or Bahrainis."}, {"id": "3:83/q11/p3", "position": "Universal wording may have particular earthly referents.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan says general wording is intended particularly; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes not everyone converts by the sword, and Abū Ḥayyān prefers heavenly universality but earthly particularity."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q12", "question": "How does 'to Him all submit' relate to the rebuking question?", "turns_on": "Whether it functions as one circumstance, emphasizes exclusive direction, or splits heaven from earth.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q12/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause: seeking another religion is absurd while all submit to God.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī supply the rhetorical force; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls the clause proof of the implied conclusion."}, {"id": "3:83/q12/p2", "position": "Placing 'to Him' first stresses exclusive submission to God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī notes the exclusive force; al-Rāzī relates it to one necessary existent and sole creative power."}, {"id": "3:83/q12/p3", "position": "The heaven clause can end before a new clause begins about the earth.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and ʿIkrima segment the wording this way."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q13", "question": "What do 'willingly' and 'unwillingly' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast concerns inner obedience or liked and disliked divine decrees.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q13/p1", "position": "They contrast easy willing obedience with submission amid difficulty, reluctance, or inner resistance.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and al-Qurṭubī distinguish ease and strain. Al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī derive ṭawʿ from yielding and cite Ibn al-Sikkīt's equivalent verbs; al-Samīn distinguishes obeying a command from agreeing."}, {"id": "3:83/q13/p2", "position": "The willing accept welcome decrees; the unwilling endure illness, poverty, or death.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās contrasts healthy and sick; al-Rāzī applies both states even to the righteous; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī stresses like and dislike."}, {"id": "3:83/q13/p3", "position": "Two vowelings of karh are dialectal; one account reserves ḍamma for hardship and fatḥa for unwilling action.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī accepts both."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q14", "question": "What is the syntax of ṭawʿan wa-karhan?", "turns_on": "Whether they are parsed as circumstantial verbal nouns or broadly called adverbs.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q14/p1", "position": "Both accusative verbal nouns function circumstantially, meaning 'willingly and unwillingly'.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Ṭabrisī compare 'he came running'; al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī explain why speech cannot be a mode of coming. Al-Samīn reports the submission/obedience analysis but objects that it fits ṭawʿan and not karhan."}, {"id": "3:83/q14/p2", "position": "They are adverbial descriptions of submission in either state.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī uses the broad adverbial description."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q15", "question": "How is karhan read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q15/p1", "position": "Al-Aʿmash reads it with ḍamma on the kāf; fatḥa is also attested.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī calls the forms dialectal; al-Samīn notes related readings elsewhere from al-Akhawayn, Kufans, and Ibn Dhakwān."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q16", "question": "What forms of willing and unwilling submission are described?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast points to acknowledged lordship, prostration, covenant, death, coerced conversion, distinct populations, decree, distress, worship, proof, or inward resistance.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q16/p1", "position": "Believers or sincere worshippers willingly obey; unbelievers acknowledge God as Creator or Lord while worshipping others.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliya, and ʿĀmir cite admission of creatorhood in 29:61, 31:25, 39:38, and 43:87, and of servanthood; ʿIkrima invokes compelling proof. Al-Ālūsī says this does not erase accountability."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p2", "position": "The believer prostrates willingly; the unbeliever or his shadow prostrates unwillingly.", "reasons": "Mujāhid's reports vary: sometimes a believer's face or shadow is willing, sometimes a disbeliever's shadow alone is reluctant, and one report calls both face and shadow willing. Sources cite 13:15, 16:48, and 4:19."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p3", "position": "All submit at the primordial covenant, some reluctantly.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and others cite the pledge in 7:172; al-Ṭabrisī says created states themselves point to God. Al-Bursawī urges fulfilling the covenant."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p4", "position": "Believers submit willingly; disbelievers submit only when death, danger, or punishment makes reality unavoidable, too late to benefit them.", "reasons": "Qatāda repeatedly cites 40:85; other accounts mention 40:84 or imminent death. Ibn ʿAṭiyya objects that the proposed scene occurs only in some cases, not every disbeliever."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p5", "position": "Some accept Islam willingly; others are compelled by sword, captivity, or worldly force.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and Maṭar give the general division; al-Kalbī contrasts born Muslims with captives and ʿIkrima includes Arab polytheists. The Prophet contrasts companions fearing God with others fearing the sword."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p6", "position": "Heavenly beings submit willingly; among earthly beings some willingly obey, others unwillingly.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and al-Mufaḍḍal distinguish heavens from earth; Abū Ḥayyān prefers heavenly ease and earthly struggle under duties. The lists name angels, Anṣār, ʿAbd al-Qays, Banū Sulaym, Emigrants, or Bahrainis."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p7", "position": "All creatures submit to God's irresistible created order, gladly in welcome states and reluctantly in unwelcome ones.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Kaysān say none can change its nature; al-Naḥḥās contrasts health and sickness. Al-Rāzī calls nonresistance strongest; Ibn Kathīr prefers dominion over the captives report. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says creational rather than devotional Islam; Study Quran uses this to resolve universal yet unwilling submission."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p8", "position": "People in danger turn sincerely to God, as sailors do during a storm.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī cites 29:65."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p9", "position": "All creation worships God, willingly or unwillingly.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās compares this with prostration in 22:18 and 13:15."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p10", "position": "Willing submission follows fair reflection on proofs; unwilling submission follows sword or overpowering signs.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites the mountain over Israel, Pharaoh's drowning, imminent death, and 40:84; al-Nasafī adds witnessing punishment. Abū Ḥayyān says this combines interpretations separately attributed to ʿIkrima, Maṭar, and Qatāda."}, {"id": "3:83/q16/p11", "position": "Humans and Satan submit unwillingly because self-will and pride obscure knowledge; other creation obeys willingly.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī cites Satan's boast in 7:12 and disavowals at 59:16, 8:48, and 14:22 as evidence of recognition too late to benefit him."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q17", "question": "What benefit does reluctant hypocritical submission bring?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q17/p1", "position": "A reluctant hypocrite gains no benefit from his deeds.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan states this consequence."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q18", "question": "What does the return to God mean and imply?", "turns_on": "Whether return stresses judgment, creative power, or final recognition.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q18/p1", "position": "All return after death or at resurrection for recompense; this warns seekers of another religion.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī includes Jews, Christians, and others. Al-Rāzī says no one else can harm or benefit; al-Biqāʿī says there is no escape; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls return a reason to seek Islam; Ibn Kathīr says deeds are repaid."}, {"id": "3:83/q18/p2", "position": "Return confirms that the One who created people by His will will resurrect them by His will.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Wāḥidī relate return to created dependence."}, {"id": "3:83/q18/p3", "position": "At final return every being recognizes God's religion; no other religion remains.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī gives this concluding acknowledgment."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q19", "question": "How does the return clause relate syntactically to the prior clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the return is independent or circumstantial, and what the pronouns denote.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q19/p1", "position": "It stands independently as a threat.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī list this possibility."}, {"id": "3:83/q19/p2", "position": "It coordinates with 'to Him all submit' as another circumstantial clause.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī describe the return as part of the circumstantial frame."}, {"id": "3:83/q19/p3", "position": "The third-person pronoun may refer to submitters or seekers; the second person refers to those addressed, with shifts in mixed readings.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī describe the alternatives."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q20", "question": "Which other passages clarify universal submission?", "turns_on": "Which cross-reference is used: creation's prostration, disbelievers' admissions, or covenant context.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q20/p1", "position": "Verses on all creation's prostration and glorification illuminate this universal submission.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās cites 22:18; Mujāhid and Ibn Kathīr cite 13:15 and 16:48–50, including shadows, animals, and angels; al-Rāzī cites 17:44 and 41:11, where heaven and earth answer willingly."}, {"id": "3:83/q20/p2", "position": "Other verses show disbelievers acknowledging God as Creator or admitting Him under distress.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and ʿIkrima cite 29:61, 31:25, 39:38, and 43:87; al-Shaʿbī cites sailors' appeal at 29:65; Qatāda cites 40:85 on useless late faith."}, {"id": "3:83/q20/p3", "position": "The covenant and command to affirm messengers connect this verse with its neighbors.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj invokes 3:85; al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī invoke 3:81; al-Sāmarrāʾī links 3:81, 3:83, and 3:85."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q21", "question": "What theological claim does universal submission support?", "turns_on": "Whether the universal wording supports metaphysical dependence, accountable agency, or obedience.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q21/p1", "position": "Everything besides God depends on Him to exist and cease; He alone is necessarily existent and creates every kind of being.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī calls this strongest and cites 13:15 and 17:44; Kur'an Yolu repeats the contingency argument."}, {"id": "3:83/q21/p2", "position": "God's decree over unbelievers does not erase responsibility for disbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī rejects the determinist inference."}, {"id": "3:83/q21/p3", "position": "No one can resist divine authority, so defying God's messengers and commands is untenable.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī notes even powerful people with allies are helpless; Ibn Kathīr speaks of irresistible dominion."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q22", "question": "How is this verse treated in verse-end counting?", "turns_on": "Whether this ending is counted and how such endings are named.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q22/p1", "position": "Verse counters omit this ending though analogous endings count for harmony with surrounding endings.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān and al-Itqān compare 3:190, 18:15, 20:80, and 5:50. Al-Itqān defines fāṣila as a beautifying pause separating statements."}, {"id": "3:83/q22/p2", "position": "Qur'anic endings are fawāṣil, not poetic rhymes; whether sajʿ may name them is disputed.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān reports consensus against qāfiya and a majority against sajʿ because of its origin and lack of authorization. Al-Rummānī's Ashʿarī distinction says fawāṣil follow meaning, whereas sajʿ forces meaning to fit."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q23", "question": "What occasion prompted this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the occasion was a dispute over Abraham or a question about prostration; al-Rāzī objects that the dispute report severs the contextual link.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q23/p1", "position": "The People of the Book disputed before the Prophet over which followed Abraham, rejected his judgment that neither did, and the verse was revealed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is named by al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, and others. Al-Qurṭubī specifies Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and companions against Christians; al-Jishumī says revelation continued through 3:85."}, {"id": "3:83/q23/p2", "position": "A man asked whether people might prostrate to the Prophet; he forbade prostration to anyone but God and the verse followed.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī transmits al-Ḥasan's account, including the direction to honor people and give them their due."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q24", "question": "What inward meanings are drawn from this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether surrender is explained by unveiled vision, effacement, enabling grace, or prophetic following.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q24/p1", "position": "Willing surrender is unobstructed vision; reluctant surrender occurs amid ego, veils, doubt, and attachment to intermediaries.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn distinguishes beholding the Essence from beholding awe. Sufi authorities cited by al-Ālūsī contrast angels and elect people with hesitant seekers and relate unbelievers' creator-acknowledgment to self-darkness; Kur'an Yolu repeats this."}, {"id": "3:83/q24/p2", "position": "The seeker must hold fast to God alone and be effaced under His decree; independent reliance leads to error.", "reasons": "Al-Wāsiṭī treats attachment beyond the One as misplaced worship. Al-Qushayrī likens independent worth to a mirage, false calculation to a barren valley, and warns against seeking God through other than Him."}, {"id": "3:83/q24/p3", "position": "Faith, knowledge, and obedience occur through God's disclosure and enabling rather than autonomous strength.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī says people know God through His teaching and affirm revelation through His enabling. Al-Shādhilī calls obedience with effaced self-awareness a blessing."}, {"id": "3:83/q24/p4", "position": "Deeds are accepted through following the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī reports that no deed is accepted outside his banner."}]}
{"id": "3:83/q25", "question": "What recitation is recommended for a difficult being?", "turns_on": "Whether the reported use is limited to mounts or extends to people and children.", "positions": [{"id": "3:83/q25/p1", "position": "Recite this verse in a stubborn mount's ear to make it tractable by God's permission.", "reasons": "Mujāhid transmits Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Durr records Yūnus ibn ʿUbayd; al-Itqān records al-Bayhaqī's Ibn ʿAbbās report."}, {"id": "3:83/q25/p2", "position": "Recite it in the ear of an ill-tempered enslaved person, animal, or child.", "reasons": "Al-Durr transmits this as a Prophetic instruction through Anas."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q01", "question": "Whom does “O people” address?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is read by its general definite plural and shared rationale, or narrowed by its later reference to Arab appeals.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q01/p1", "position": "All accountable people addressed by the revelation, including women and later generations", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī cites the definite plural, universal creation, and universal duty of taqwā; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī tie the address to shared origin; al-Ālūsī excludes past generations unable to comply."}, {"id": "4:1/q01/p2", "position": "The people of Mecca or Arabs who invoked God and kinship", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās grounds the restriction in Arab invocation custom; al-Rāzī replies that a particular final clause need not narrow the opening."}, {"id": "4:1/q01/p3", "position": "Believers or unbelievers and hypocrites specifically", "reasons": "Saʿīd b. Jubayr calls the warning one to believers; Ibn ʿAbbās in Ibn Abī Ḥātim identifies unbelievers and hypocrites; Abū Ḥayyān cites believers' brotherhood."}, {"id": "4:1/q01/p4", "position": "All Adam's children, including earlier peoples", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports an eternal-speech rationale but objects that the command's revealed legal force cannot bind earlier peoples."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q02", "question": "How does the opening vocative work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q02/p1", "position": "Yā calls, ayy is the singular vocative, hā alerts, and al-nās specifies or modifies ayy", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās notes yā can be omitted when the addressee is known; al-Akhfash instead treats ayy as a relative pronoun."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q03", "question": "What does the command to fear the Lord require?", "turns_on": "The breadth of taqwā in the command and whether it is read as general duty, social duty, or an inward state.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q03/p1", "position": "Obey God and avoid disobedience, sins, and His punishment", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī stresses commands and prohibitions; Ibn ʿAbbās glosses obedience, Muqātil fear, and al-Ṭabrisī adds avoiding neglect of God's due."}, {"id": "4:1/q03/p2", "position": "Protect mutual rights and maintain human ties", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Ālūsī say common descent frames the sūra's obligations toward kin, orphans, women, and spouses."}, {"id": "4:1/q03/p3", "position": "Inwardly, avoid all that diverts from God and purify intention", "reasons": "Al-Sulamī gives levels from avoiding shirk through leaving reliance on deeds; al-Qushayrī names the self as the first 'other'; al-Bursawī distinguishes three levels."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q04", "question": "Why is God called “your Lord” here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q04/p1", "position": "The title evokes ownership, creation, nurture, and benefaction, which warrant obedience", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya glosses rabb as owner; al-Rāzī argues lordship and servitude entail submission; al-Biqāʿī and Elmalılı emphasize nurture."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q05", "question": "How is “who created you” related to the command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q05/p1", "position": "Creation establishes God's power to punish and His blessings that demand grateful obedience", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Bayḍāwī, and al-Ālūsī give both power and favor; al-Rāzī adds that creation makes God master and enables obedience itself."}, {"id": "4:1/q05/p2", "position": "The creation account also grounds social care through shared origin", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says all people owe sibling-like care; al-Rāzī applies it especially to the weak; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees protection of social unity."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q06", "question": "How is “created you” parsed and what does creation mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q06/p1", "position": "The relative adjective qualifies “your Lord,” and min marks origin in creating the addressed people", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās gives the imperative and adjective case; al-Samīn calls min nafs an accusative complement and min the starting point."}, {"id": "4:1/q06/p2", "position": "The verse does not establish that every creation requires prior matter", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī's theologians argue that creation of something distinct from matter is from nonexistence; al-Ālūsī says the verse states only human origins."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q07", "question": "How is خلقكم pronounced at the qāf–kāf junction?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q07/p1", "position": "Most pronounce qāf and kāf distinctly; some assimilate qāf into kāf", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī says their shared point of articulation allows assimilation."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q08", "question": "Who or what is the one soul?", "turns_on": "Whether nafs denotes a particular ancestor, a generic human origin, or an inward archetype.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q08/p1", "position": "Adam, the particular first human and common ancestor", "reasons": "Numerous early reports name Adam; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites the two parents of 7:27 and Adam's children in 17:62, and says a generic reading loses the force of 'one' in 4:1."}, {"id": "4:1/q08/p2", "position": "Humanity or a living entity in a common-origin sense, without identifying an individual Adam", "reasons": "ʿAbduh and Asad seek a statement of brotherhood without commitment to the Biblical narrative; some exegetes take every person's parents generically, but al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that the verse speaks of one original source."}, {"id": "4:1/q08/p3", "position": "Inwardly, the universal rational soul or Muhammadan Reality", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī calls it the world's heart and real Adam; al-Ālūsī calls it father of historical Adam; an unusual view reported by Abū Ḥayyān calls it spirit paired with body."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q09", "question": "Why does wāḥidah have a feminine ending, and is wāḥid read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q09/p1", "position": "Wāḥidah agrees with the feminine noun nafs though Adam is male; masculine wāḥid is possible by sense and is also read", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, and others cite semantic agreement and poetry; Ibn Abī ʿAblah's reading has wāḥid, and al-Samīn notes nafs can itself be masculine."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q10", "question": "What does nafs mean as a word?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q10/p1", "position": "A person or thing itself; a human self can include body and spirit", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives the basic lexical sense; Kur'an Yolu also gives living element continuing after death and recounts views identifying or distinguishing nafs and spirit."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q11", "question": "Does this verse imply one Adam or earlier human cycles?", "turns_on": "Whether transmitted reports, creation verses, or proposed scientific inferences establish prior human kinds or cycles.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q11/p1", "position": "This Adam is humanity's first ancestor, with no earlier humans like him", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī states the mainstream Sunni view and rejects an eternal human species; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī holds that the current lineage begins with Adam and Eve."}, {"id": "4:1/q11/p2", "position": "Other Adams or earlier worlds may have preceded this Adam", "reasons": "Reports in Jāmiʿ al-Akhbār, al-Tawḥīd, and al-Khiṣāl give thirty or a million Adams and twelve thousand worlds; al-Ālūsī suggests other worlds need not mean prior humans here. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds the Qurʾān noncommittal about earlier cycles."}, {"id": "4:1/q11/p3", "position": "Humanity arose by development from earlier life forms", "reasons": "Researchers cite increasing complexity and limited observed development; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says no experiment demonstrates change of species into humanity."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q12", "question": "What can be inferred about the age of humanity?", "turns_on": "How much chronological weight is assigned to traditional reports, demographic estimates, and ancient remains.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q12/p1", "position": "A seven-thousand-year chronology is reported", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports a six-thousand-year span before the Prophet and a seven-thousand-year world; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī outlines Jewish tradition and a demographic model, including severe mortality."}, {"id": "4:1/q12/p2", "position": "The chronology is unknown or much older evidence exists", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says reports conflict and God alone knows; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports geologists' ancient fossils but says they do not establish uninterrupted descent."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q14", "question": "What was Eve created from?", "turns_on": "Whether min is bodily partitive, points to common kind or clay, or marks another proposed substance.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q14/p1", "position": "From Adam himself, especially a rib", "reasons": "Mujāhid specifies the short rib during sleep; al-Suddī places Adam alone in Paradise; Ibn Isḥāq specifies the left rib. Prophetic rib reports counsel gentle treatment; al-Qāḍī argues an independent Eve would imply two original souls."}, {"id": "4:1/q14/p2", "position": "From Adam's kind or the same human nature, without requiring a rib", "reasons": "Abū Muslim cites 16:72, 3:164, and 9:128; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites other same-kind spouse verses and says this verse supplies no rib proof; modern writers treat rib reports figuratively."}, {"id": "4:1/q14/p3", "position": "From the leftover clay of Adam's creation", "reasons": "Abū Jaʿfar al-Bāqir and a reported Prophetic answer reject the rib account and specify leftover or same superior clay."}, {"id": "4:1/q14/p4", "position": "A heavenly maiden of the same substance as houris", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports and rejects this for lack of Qurʾānic or hadith support."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q15", "question": "When was Eve created relative to entering Paradise?", "turns_on": "The divergent reports about the place and sequence of Eve's creation.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q15/p1", "position": "After Adam entered Paradise, while he slept", "reasons": "Reports from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and others describe his sleep, rib removal, and waking recognition; some specify left, others right."}, {"id": "4:1/q15/p2", "position": "Before Adam entered Paradise", "reasons": "Kaʿb al-Aḥbār, Wahb, and Ibn Isḥāq are named for this report."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q16", "question": "How are the creation clauses joined syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether wāw joins the preceding finite verb directly or an understood clause or verbal sense.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q16/p1", "position": "They coordinate directly with “created you”; wāw does not require chronological order", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn reject a needed ellipsis; Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the clauses as successive qualifications detailing one wondrous creation."}, {"id": "4:1/q16/p2", "position": "An omitted “He created Adam” precedes “and created his spouse”", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī inserts the clause to preserve the historical sequence; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī report it; Abū Ḥayyān says it is unnecessary."}, {"id": "4:1/q16/p3", "position": "“Created her spouse” coordinates with wāḥidah understood as “made single”", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives the verbal sense of wāḥidah and cites the verb waḥada as support."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q17", "question": "What variant reads the creation and spreading verbs as participles?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q17/p1", "position": "Khāliq and bāthth are read as participles with an omitted subject “He”", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, and al-Samīn parse them as predicates of huwa."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q18", "question": "What does baththa mean?", "turns_on": "Whether a contextual gloss states the act of creation or its dispersal.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q18/p1", "position": "To spread, scatter, or disperse widely; in context to propagate people", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj note abaththa as another form; 101:4 compares scattering moths, 88:16 spread carpets, and poetry uses the verb for disclosing secrets."}, {"id": "4:1/q18/p2", "position": "To create or bring forth, in al-Suddī's contextual gloss", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim also attributes this gloss to Muqātil b. Ḥayyān."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q19", "question": "Who are the people spread from the pair, and how?", "turns_on": "Whether the dual source exhausts the ancestry of all presently living humans.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q19/p1", "position": "All human descendants arose through reproduction from Adam and Eve", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and many others make the dual Adam and Eve; al-Rāzī notes descendants may be attributed to the original pair even through later generations; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī denies another contributing source."}, {"id": "4:1/q19/p2", "position": "Human origins included separate parents or later admixture", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports color and blood arguments for four original couples and a geographic argument from the Americas, but counters that variation and geological change can account for both."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q20", "question": "How did Adam and Eve's first children reproduce?", "turns_on": "Whether sole descent entails sibling marriage or leaves room for an unstated form of creation.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q20/p1", "position": "Their children married siblings under a temporary divine permission", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argues a sole first pair entails this; al-Sajjād reports cross-pair sibling marriages and a later ban; the ruling is changeable when necessity ends."}, {"id": "4:1/q20/p2", "position": "They married houris or jinn spouses", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this alternative and rejects it in favor of sibling marriage."}, {"id": "4:1/q20/p3", "position": "The verse and sound reports leave the mechanism unknown", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu notes varied miraculous creation modes for Adam, Jesus, and Yaḥyā and declines to infer sibling unions."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q21", "question": "What do reports say about Adam and Eve's children?", "turns_on": "The number and details transmitted in the distinct reports.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q21/p1", "position": "Adam had forty children, twenty boys and twenty girls, in twenty paired pregnancies", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq names Cain, Abel, Seth, and several daughters; Ibn ʿAbbās gives the count."}, {"id": "4:1/q21/p2", "position": "Eve bore Seth as Adam's third child after severe labor", "reasons": "Arṭāʾ says angels kept him forty days and taught him signs before returning him."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q22", "question": "Why mention many men and women in this form?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective is shared by ellipsis, intentionally restricted, or part of a hierarchy in ordering.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q22/p1", "position": "The wording conveys vast human multiplication; “many” after men also covers women", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says baththa and the first adjective make women's abundance clear; al-Samīn reports ellipsis; al-Bayḍāwī and al-Bursawī say women may be more numerous."}, {"id": "4:1/q22/p2", "position": "Many qualifies men alone because men are publicly prominent while women are concealed", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, and al-Samīn report this; al-Biqāʿī also associates the order with visible strength."}, {"id": "4:1/q22/p3", "position": "Men are named first as a mark of rank or prominence", "reasons": "Al-Burhān compares other Qurʾānic orderings; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives a distinct sex-symbolic inward reading."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q23", "question": "How does “many” work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether kathīr qualifies the expressed noun or an understood verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q23/p1", "position": "It modifies rijāl and keeps one form with a plural noun", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 3:146; Abū al-Baqāʾ explains masculine agreement through the collective sense of men."}, {"id": "4:1/q23/p2", "position": "It modifies an omitted verbal noun, meaning a great dispersal", "reasons": "Al-Samīn cites Sībawayh's circumstantial analysis; al-Ālūsī calls the analysis strained."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q24", "question": "Do “men and women” exclude a third human sex?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q24/p1", "position": "An intersex person is not a third kind but belongs in reality to one of the two", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, and Abū Ḥayyān make the inference from the division into men and women."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q25", "question": "How is tasāʾalūna read and formed?", "turns_on": "The phonological treatment of the two tāʾs, and separate simple-verb forms.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q25/p1", "position": "With a doubled sīn through assimilation of tāʾ in tatasāʾalūn", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and Ibn ʿĀmir are named; Abū ʿAmr varies by transmission. Al-Fārisī says tāʾ and sīn are close and voiceless; the meaning is unchanged."}, {"id": "4:1/q25/p2", "position": "With a light sīn through deletion of one tāʾ", "reasons": "ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and many Kufans read it; explanations differ over which tāʾ drops. Abū ʿAlī cites deletion, assimilation, and substitution as strategies, with ṭast and poetry as examples."}, {"id": "4:1/q25/p3", "position": "With a simple verb tasʾalūn or taslūn", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's form lacks the long alif; another transfers the hamza's vowel to sīn. The simple form supports direct asking rather than reciprocal asking."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q26", "question": "What does asking one another by God mean?", "turns_on": "The social act denoted by mutual asking: petition, contract, or affectionate invocation.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q26/p1", "position": "People invoke God's name in requests for needs or rights", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī quotes “I ask/adjure you by God”; al-Zajjāj says it seeks rights; al-Rāzī says God's name strengthens plea, request, or oath."}, {"id": "4:1/q26/p2", "position": "People make covenants, contracts, or pledges by God", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ give this gloss; Ibn ʿAbbās in al-Durr says “transact by Him.”"}, {"id": "4:1/q26/p3", "position": "The phrase speaks of mutual affection through God", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās supplies this gloss."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q28", "question": "How is al-arḥām read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Case ending, coordination to a bound pronoun, omitted preposition or verb, and whether wāw is conjunctive or an oath.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q28/p1", "position": "Accusative: object of the fear command, an omitted injunction, or the syntactic position of bihi", "reasons": "Most readers use fatḥa; the common command is to maintain kinship. Al-Wāḥidī, Abū ʿAlī, and others also analyze it as an object coordinated with the position of bihi and cite poetry or Ibn Masʿūd's explicit bi."}, {"id": "4:1/q28/p2", "position": "Genitive: coordinate kinship with bihi or supply an omitted bi, so it too is invoked", "reasons": "Ḥamza and several early readers use kasra. {"id": "4:1/q29", "question": "What objections and defenses concern the genitive reading?", "turns_on": "Whether a grammatical school's analogy can restrict a transmitted reading, and whether invocation counts as swearing.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q29/p1", "position": "Basran grammar finds coordination to a bound genitive pronoun weak or impermissible", "reasons": "Sībawayh allows it in poetic necessity only; al-Māzinī says conjuncts must be interchangeable; Abū ʿAlī compares bound pronouns to tanwīn; al-Zajjāj adds the ban on swearing by other than God."}, {"id": "4:1/q29/p2", "position": "Kufan usage and authenticated reading permit the construction or an understood bi", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says transmitted language outranks anonymous poetry and weak analogy; Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Māzinī's reciprocity test; al-Ālūsī separates an appeal by kinship from a prohibited oath."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q30", "question": "What does al-arḥām mean and what is its root?", "turns_on": "The lexical extension from womb to family and proposed etymological relation to mercy.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q30/p1", "position": "Wombs, by extension kinship and relatives sharing descent", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī gives a container–content extension; al-Ālūsī includes distant blood relatives; al-Naḥḥās notes the noun's feminine gender and vocalic forms."}, {"id": "4:1/q30/p2", "position": "The noun derives from raḥma, mercy, or the womb; an independent-root view also exists", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports the three derivations and calls the disagreement minor; a divine report links raḥim to al-Raḥmān."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q31", "question": "What does the kinship clause require?", "turns_on": "Whether arḥām is governed by a command to preserve kin or belongs to the customary appeal.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q31/p1", "position": "Maintain relatives' rights and do not sever them", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, al-Suddī and many later exegetes give this command; Ibn Zayd cites 13:21, and al-Ṭabrisī includes acknowledging lineage and financial support."}, {"id": "4:1/q31/p2", "position": "The verse describes people invoking both God and kinship in appeals", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan gives 'I adjure you by God and kin'; al-Wāḥidī notes Arab and polytheist custom; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that this syntactic treatment may imply an improper equality."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q32", "question": "What legal duties follow for kinship?", "turns_on": "Which relatives are covered and what legal consequences follow from the command.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q32/p1", "position": "Maintaining kinship is obligatory, severing it forbidden, even for non-Muslim relatives", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports agreement across religious communities and cites the Prophet's order to Asmāʾ to maintain her unbelieving mother; reports promise long life and divine connection."}, {"id": "4:1/q32/p2", "position": "Possession of a close blood relative triggers emancipation; views differ on scope", "reasons": "Ḥanafīs and many early authorities include unmarriageable relatives; al-Shāfiʿī restricts to parents and children; Literalists resist automatic freedom. Al-Qurṭubī favors the wider rule and discusses the contested Ibn ʿUmar report and milk kin."}, {"id": "4:1/q32/p3", "position": "Kinship can bar revoking gifts and support relatives' inheritance; the scope is disputed", "reasons": "Ḥanafīs protect gifts to unmarriageable kin and give inheritance to relatives absent standard heirs; al-Qurṭubī objects that excluding cousins narrows the verse without proof."}, {"id": "4:1/q32/p4", "position": "An appeal by God's name should be honored", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī derives permissibility of asking by God and cites reports to give such a petitioner and honor an oath."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q33", "question": "What reports illustrate the reward and reality of kinship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q33/p1", "position": "Kinship is depicted at or under the Throne, asking connection for those who connect and severance for those who sever", "reasons": "Reports appear from Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Hurayra, ʿAlī, and others; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains the Throne image through the reality of the social bond and its cosmic effects."}, {"id": "4:1/q33/p2", "position": "Maintaining kinship is said to extend life and bring quick reward; severance, oppression, and false oaths bring quick harm", "reasons": "Reports from Qatāda, Ibn ʿAbbās, Anas, and others are cited; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī also suggests practical family solidarity as a cause of longevity."}, {"id": "4:1/q33/p3", "position": "Drawing near to and touching an angry relative calms anger", "reasons": "ʿAlī and al-Ṣādiq report the practice; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explains its attentional and natural-affection effects."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q34", "question": "Why is the command to fear God repeated, and why use Allah here?", "turns_on": "Whether repetition chiefly intensifies the same command or distinguishes its grounds and tone.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q34/p1", "position": "Repetition reinforces the command and draws attention to kinship duties", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Rāzī, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī make this point."}, {"id": "4:1/q34/p2", "position": "Rabb first evokes favor and nurture; Allah next evokes majesty, awe, and legislation", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguish encouragement through creation from legislative warning; al-Ālūsī says the proper name invokes all divine perfections."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q35", "question": "What does raqīb mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q35/p1", "position": "A vigilant guardian and watcher who knows, preserves, and records deeds", "reasons": "Mujāhid and Ibn ʿAbbās gloss ḥafīẓ; Ibn Zayd stresses knowledge. Abū Duwād's watchman poem and the arrow-game watcher support the lexical sense; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī adds surveillance toward correction and recompense."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q36", "question": "How does the closing watchfulness clause work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q36/p1", "position": "It gives the reason for obedience: God continuously watches all outer and inner acts", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say kāna does not confine watching to the past; ʿalaykum makes the warning direct; al-Ālūsī notes explicit Allah and fronting for rhyme."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q37", "question": "Where and when was Sūrat al-Nisāʾ revealed, and how many verses has it?", "turns_on": "How a sūra with material of different dates is classified, and differing regional verse division.", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q37/p1", "position": "It is Medinan, with a reported Meccan exception or later passages; regional counts range from 175 to 177", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha says al-Baqara and al-Nisāʾ came after she joined the Prophet; 4:58 at Mecca need not reclassify the sūra; al-Jishumī and al-Ālūsī give Syrian 177, Kufan 176, others 175."}, {"id": "4:1/q37/p2", "position": "It is Meccan or was revealed around the Migration", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports the Meccan view from ʿAṭiyya via Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Jābir b. {"id": "4:1/q38", "question": "What virtues and liturgical uses of this verse or sūra are reported?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q38/p1", "position": "The Prophet recited 4:1 with 59:18 to urge charity for destitute arrivals", "reasons": "Jarīr describes the Mudar group, an Anṣārī's initiating gift, and the community's food and clothing; the sermon teaches shared reward or burden for starting practices."}, {"id": "4:1/q38/p2", "position": "The Prophet included 4:1 among three verses in the sermon of need", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd's report gives praise, appeal for aid and forgiveness, confession of faith, then 4:1, 3:102, and a verse of 33; al-Nasāʾī notes chain disconnections."}, {"id": "4:1/q38/p3", "position": "Reports praise recitation of al-Nisāʾ or the seven long sūras", "reasons": "Ubayy's attributed promise lists charity, inheritance, emancipation, and safety from shirk; other reports call mastery of seven long sūras learning and describe extended recitation."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q41", "question": "How does shared human origin encourage concord?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q41/p1", "position": "People should practice affection, humility, and mutual care because they share one human ancestor", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān stresses natural affinity and repudiation of pride; the common origin also supports the duties of the sūra."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q43", "question": "What signs of prophecy and unity does creation from one soul provide?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q43/p1", "position": "The remarkable shared origin displays divine unity and power, while an unlettered Prophet's knowledge of it supports his prophethood", "reasons": "Al-Aṣamm says unaided reason cannot establish this unseen origin; Abū Ḥayyān notes the Prophet had no prior scriptural instruction and says branching descent defeats materialist claims."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q44", "question": "What does the verse teach about resurrection, pride, and human diversity?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q44/p1", "position": "Diverse humanity from one origin demonstrates divine power to resurrect and undermines pride and rivalry", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān follows al-Rāzī in arguing that re-creation is no harder than origination, and common ancestry calls for humility."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q45", "question": "How do the Adam and Eve reports bear on a literal or figurative rib?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q45/p1", "position": "A sound rib report is cited for bodily origin, while a figurative reading treats the rib as an image of temperamental difference", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the Adam and Eve identification and Ibn ʿAṭiyya's sound hadith; he allows the figurative comparison, while al-Qāḍī argues the single origin favors a literal derivation."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q46", "question": "Why might Eve's creation from Adam have taken this form?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q46/p1", "position": "It displays creation of life from life, creates mutual desire and companionship, and prepares reproduction", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says the original part's identity ceased and reports Ibn ʿArabī's account of a void attracting Adam to Eve; he also says the pair may be unique among animals and the addressees' creation is fronted for exhortation."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q47", "question": "What additional rhetorical figures occur in this passage?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q47/p1", "position": "The passage uses antithesis, ellipsis, and repetition", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān identifies contrasts of one and mate, rich and poor, few and many; he notes omitted elements and recurring fear, creation, women, orphans, inheritance, and guarding."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q48", "question": "How does a first mention of taqwā relate to rights of others?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q48/p1", "position": "It can be a general avoidance of punishment or a focused warning to protect others' rights", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān contrasts the readings; al-Ālūsī describes broad piety as avoiding unbelief, sin, and vice alongside divine and human rights."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q49", "question": "What does the appeal to God's name imply for obedience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q49/p1", "position": "The appeal treats God's name as weighty, so people should obey the One invoked", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān notes appeals by God and kinship together; al-Ālūsī says such entreaty calls for keeping God's commands."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q50", "question": "What further reasons support care for kinship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q50/p1", "position": "The command joins a specific human right to reverence for God, backed by scriptural parallels and the kinship bond's reality", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān sees a common sense of avoiding violation and cites 2:83 and 2:27; al-Ālūsī says the second exhortation can specify what the first includes."}]}
{"id": "4:1/q51", "question": "What further objections were made to coordinating al-arḥām with a bound pronoun?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q51/p1", "position": "Some grammarians object to the tight preposition–pronoun unit and to the implications for swearing", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī's unit argument and Ibn ʿAṭiyya's Basran, poetic-exception, inseparability, exhortative-value, and oath objections."}]}

{"id": "4:1/q54", "question": "How are other reading details in the verse explained?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "4:1/q54/p1", "position": "A participial creation reading and assimilated asking form are reported; the nouns for the offspring can denote both sexes at all ages", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī describes the two-tāʾ source of the ordinary form, its omission and assimilation, and the wording's picture of each descendant as a potential ancestor."}]}
